title: The Harmandir's day
hookLine: the Granth is carried in a palki to rest at night and returned at dawn

lines: A DRUM, A CONCH, A CROWD.
cards: Amritsar, before first light. The water around the Harmandir Sahib is black and flat, and the gold looks almost gray.
People wait along the causeway, some barefoot on cold marble, some with children asleep on their shoulders. Then a drum, and a conch, and the crowd begins to move.
Hands reach out to touch the poles of something being carried. A palki, a palanquin, is coming home. Inside it is a book, wrapped in cloth, and the people reaching for it call that book the Guru.
This path has watched the night crossing once already. Today, the whole day around it.

teach.b: Begin before the light. In the Japji, Guru Nanak points to the ambrosial hours, the early dark before dawn, in paraphrase: in those hours, dwell on the true Name and its greatness. The Harmandir's day starts there.

The Granth is carried from its night room, set on its high seat under a canopy, and opened. Sikhs call this the prakash, the light. A hymn is read from the opened page: the Guru's word for that morning.
Then the long middle. All day, singers take turns in the sanctum, set after set, while people cross the causeway, bow, listen for a moment, and move on. The doors stay open.
The kitchen keeps feeding. The Guru is, in Sikh language, holding court. Then night.
After the evening prayers, the Granth is closed, wrapped, and carried out in the palki to rest. Sikhs call this sukhasan, the seat of ease. Not storage.
Rest. So why carry a book to bed?

teach.h: PRAKASH: THE GURU OPENED FOR THE DAY.
teach.b: Because Sikhs treat the Guru Granth Sahib not as a book they own but as the living Guru, the one Guru Gobind Singh named before he died.

teach.h: ALL DAY, THE HYMNS SUNG ON.
teach.b: A living Guru wakes, gives the word, keeps company, and rests.
The ritual is about how you'd treat someone you revere if they lived in your house.

teach.h: A LIVING GURU WAKES AND RESTS.
teach.b: Gurdwaras do a version of this in a quiet back room, and so do homes that keep the Granth. At the Harmandir it happens in front of the crowd.

how: At the Harmandir Sahib the Guru Granth Sahib is brought out in a palki before dawn for the prakash and carried back at night for sukhasan; gurdwaras and homes that keep the Granth follow the same pattern on a smaller scale.

games.q: you've traveled to Amritsar and want to see the Guru Granth Sahib arrive for the day. when do you go to the causeway?
o: at midnight, after it's been put to rest.
games.why: before dawn the palki comes back across the causeway, and the Granth is opened for the day.

practice: See the causeway in the dark, the palki on the shoulders of the crowd, the drum and the conch; then the evening, the same palki going the other way, and between the two crossings a whole day of hymns.
Breathe in at the dawn crossing and out at the night one, resting on Waheguru if you pray.

wordCard.voice: The Harmandir's day. The Granth opened at dawn in the prakash, sung all day, and carried at night in the palki to rest, in sukhasan. Today's word.

orig.note: Punjabi: the seat of ease; the Guru Granth Sahib put to rest for the night.
